                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §
                                                                       OF TEXAS
                                                  §
                                                  §

                           CHOLLA, INC’S INITIAL COMMENTS

                                       I.     Introduction

       Cholla, Inc. (“Cholla”) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on proposed 16
Tex. Admin. Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 implementing Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) §
37.0561 regarding interconnection standards for large load customers in the ERCOT region. As a
developer of large-scale load infrastructure in Texas, Cholla is committed to supporting a reliable,
efficient, and transparent interconnection framework that enables continued economic growth
while maintaining system integrity.

       Cholla supports the Commission’s objective of ensuring that large load interconnection
requests are grounded in demonstrably viable and committed projects. The scale and pace of large
load development in ERCOT necessitate a structured framework that appropriately balances
business development, system reliability, and protection of existing customers. In particular, the
transition toward a coordinated or batch study process represents a meaningful and necessary
evolution in transmission planning.

       At the same time, targeted refinements to the proposed rule are necessary to ensure that
financial requirements remain appropriately calibrated, non-duplicative, and closely aligned with
actual system risk and cost incurrence. As currently structured, certain provisions—particularly
those governing financial security at the intermediate agreement stage and the treatment of retained
funds—introduce outcomes that are not closely tied to cost causation or stranded infrastructure
risk and that may have broader implications for transmission cost recovery.

       These comments focus on two interdependent aspects of the proposed framework: (i) the
non-refundable structure of financial security prior to completion of interconnection studies, and
(ii) the required treatment of retained funds in a manner that affects transmission rate base. As


                                                 1
 discussed below, the interaction of these elements results in a financial structure that extends
beyond project-specific interconnection cost recovery and introduces unintended economic and
structural effects.

        Cholla respectfully submits that these issues can be addressed through targeted
refinement—without altering the overall structure or objectives of the rule—to ensure that the final
framework remains consistent with PURA § 37.0561, grounded in cost-causation principles, and
capable of supporting continued investment in large load infrastructure while maintaining system
reliability.

               II.    Structural Concerns with Proposed Financial Framework

A.      Ratemaking Implications of Proposed Financial Treatment

        As proposed in Staff’s Proposal for Publication (“PFP”), § 25.194 includes provisions that
extend beyond the establishment of interconnection standards and, as structured, introduce
elements that constitute ratemaking in substance by determining how funds are applied to rate base
outside of a PURA Chapter 36 proceeding.

        In particular, the rule requires that certain payments collected from large load customers—
including amounts derived from financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage—be
transferred to the interconnecting Transmission Service Provider (“TSP”) and applied as an offset
to the TSP’s rate base in a future rate proceeding. As a result, those amounts no longer function
solely as mechanisms to ensure recovery of project-specific interconnection costs or to protect
against stranded infrastructure risk. Instead, they directly affect the level of transmission system
costs ultimately recovered from ratepayers. In practice, many large load interconnection requests
are initiated by developers or project sponsors that are not themselves the ultimate end-use
customer and may never take service on the ERCOT system. The rule therefore requires entities
that are not customers of the ERCOT system—and may never become customers—to fund
transmission system costs through forfeited financial security.

        Under PURA Chapter 36, ratemaking is governed by a structured framework. The
Commission is authorized to establish and regulate rates and to determine customer classifications




                                                 2
 and applicability of rates. 1 Rates must be just and reasonable and may not be unreasonably
preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. 2 In setting rates, the Commission must establish the
utility’s overall revenue requirement at a level that provides a reasonable opportunity to earn a
return on invested capital used and useful in providing service. 3 This process necessarily includes
determination of revenues and expenses and the allocation of costs in accordance with established
ratemaking principles. 4

       Although the Commission retains authority to adopt rules that may influence ratemaking
outcomes, as proposed, 16 TAC § 25.194 effectively prescribes the treatment of specific funds
within future rate base calculations without the benefit of those procedural and evidentiary
safeguards. In a ratemaking context, the utility bears the burden of demonstrating that proposed
rates are just and reasonable. 5 By contrast, the proposed rule would predetermine that certain
payments are applied to reduce rate base outside of that framework.

       This concern is further underscored by the statutory requirement that rate base be grounded
in property that is used and useful in providing service. 6 To the extent payments collected from
large load customers are retained and applied to reduce transmission rate base irrespective of
whether they correspond to used and useful utility investment, they function as a system-wide cost
recovery mechanism rather than a project-specific interconnection safeguard. This disconnect
further demonstrates that the retained funds are not tied to specific utility investment used and
useful in providing service, but instead operate as a generalized funding mechanism.

       These ratemaking implications should be considered in light of the statutory framework
under which this rule is adopted. PURA § 35.004 requires that large load customers contribute to
the recovery of the utility’s costs to interconnect that customer, and PURA § 37.0561 directs the
Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business development, minimize
stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain system reliability. These provisions are focused on



1
  PURA § 36.001.
2
  PURA § 36.003.
3
  PURA § 36.051.
4
  PURA §§ 36.055, 36.057.
5
  PURA § 36.006.
6
  PURA § 36.053.


                                                 3
 project-specific cost recovery and risk mitigation. To the extent the proposed rule results in
retention of funds that are not tied to interconnection cost recovery or stranded cost exposure and
directs their application to rate base, it extends beyond those purposes and implicates broader
transmission cost recovery considerations typically addressed under PURA Chapter 36.

        Cholla does not dispute the Commission’s authority to determine rate base treatment under
PURA Chapter 36. However, that authority must be exercised within a ratemaking proceeding, not
through an interconnection standards rule. Ratemaking proceedings require the development of a
cost-of-service record, the establishment of a utility’s revenue requirement, the allocation of costs
among customer classes, and the determination of just and reasonable rates. Because this
proceeding does not include those elements, it cannot be used to establish or predetermine recovery
of transmission system costs.


        Accordingly, Cholla recommends that the Commission revise the proposed rule to:


     1. Limit financial requirements to amounts necessary to recover project-specific
        interconnection costs and mitigate identifiable stranded cost risk; and

     2. Remove or modify provisions that mandate specific rate base treatment of collected funds,
        preserving the ability to evaluate such treatment in a future ratemaking proceeding
        consistent with PURA Chapter 36.



B.      Non-Refundable Financial Commitments at the Intermediate Stage

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 requires large load customers to post substantial financial
security at the intermediate agreement stage—prior to initiation of the interconnection study—in
the amount of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand. This requirement, in combination with
the rule’s withdrawal and forfeiture provisions, introduces a structure that imposes material non-
refundable financial exposure before a project’s technical feasibility, cost profile, or deliverability
has been established.

        Consistent with PURA §§ 35.004 and 37.0561, financial security should be calibrated to
ensure recovery of incurred interconnection costs and protection against identifiable stranded
infrastructure risk, rather than to create independent financial exposure unrelated to those statutory


                                                  4
 objectives.

       Specifically, under § 25.194(d)(10), a large load customer must post financial security as a
condition to initiating the interconnection study. If the customer subsequently withdraws its request
or is unable to proceed—whether due to study results, system constraints, or other external
factors—the rule requires that the interconnecting utility first apply the financial security to any
outstanding costs and then refund only 20% of any remaining balance, with the remaining 80%
transferred to the TSP and applied as an offset to rate base.

       As structured, this framework results in substantial non-refundable forfeiture even in
circumstances where:
   1. No interconnection facilities have been constructed;

   2. No stranded infrastructure costs have been incurred; and

   3. The outcome of the interconnection study or broader system conditions renders the project
      infeasible or materially altered from its original assumptions.

       This allocation of risk is not aligned with the statutory objectives underlying PURA §
37.0561. That provision directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that
minimize the potential for stranded infrastructure costs while maintaining system reliability. The
financial security requirement, however, extends beyond protection against identifiable cost
exposure and instead places significant financial risk on the developer prior to the point at which
such risk can be reasonably evaluated.

       In effect, the rule requires large load customers to commit substantial capital before they
have access to the very information—study results, upgrade requirements, cost estimates, and
deliverability constraints—necessary to assess project viability. The resulting forfeiture risk is
therefore driven not by developer conduct, failure to perform, or incurred system costs, but by the
outcome of system-wide study processes and planning determinations that are outside the control
of the large load customer.

       This structure transforms financial security from a tool intended to (i) ensure cost recovery
for interconnection-related expenditures, and (ii) protect utilities and ratepayers from stranded
infrastructure risk, into a mechanism that imposes material, non-refundable financial exposure in



                                                  5
 advance of those risks being realized or even quantified.

        Moreover, because the majority of forfeited amounts are ultimately transferred to the TSP
and applied as an offset to rate base, the forfeiture is not limited to recovery of project-specific
costs, but instead operates as a broader funding mechanism affecting transmission system cost
recovery. This further underscores that the current structure is not narrowly tailored to the statutory
purposes of cost causation and stranded cost protection.

        Accordingly, Cholla recommends that the Commission revise the intermediate-stage
financial security framework to better align with PURA § 37.0561 by:
     1. Limiting non-refundable exposure at the intermediate stage to amounts directly tied to
        incurred or non-cancellable costs;

     2. Preserving a higher degree of refundability until completion of the interconnection study
        and execution of the interconnection agreement; and

     3. Ensuring that forfeiture is triggered by demonstrable cost incurrence or developer-driven
        actions, rather than by system-wide study outcomes or feasibility determinations.

        A revised structure that ties financial exposure to actual cost incurrence and project-specific
risk would maintain appropriate discipline and commitment from interconnecting customers while
avoiding unnecessary barriers to development and preserving alignment with the statutory
objectives of reliability, cost causation, and support for business development in Texas.

C.      Interaction of Financial Structure and Ratemaking Treatment

        The concerns identified above regarding (1) the ratemaking implications of the proposed
financial treatment, and (2) the non-refundable structure of financial security at the intermediate
agreement stage are not independent. Rather, they operate together as an integrated mechanism
that produces outcomes extending beyond the scope of interconnection standards contemplated
under PURA §§ 35.004 and 37.0561.

        As proposed, the rule requires large load customers to post substantial financial security
prior to the initiation of interconnection studies and, in the event of withdrawal or non-utilization,
directs that only a limited portion of the remaining balance be refunded, with the majority
transferred to the TSP and applied as an offset to rate base. This interaction between early-stage
financial commitments and downstream ratemaking treatment is central to the structure and effect


                                                  6
 of the rule.

        If financial security at the intermediate stage were structured to remain largely
refundable—subject to deduction only for demonstrable, project-specific costs incurred by the
interconnecting utility—the financial framework would function in a manner consistent with
traditional interconnection principles. In that case, financial security would serve its intended
purposes of ensuring cost recovery for interconnection-related expenditures and protecting against
stranded infrastructure risk, consistent with PURA.

        However, under proposed § 25.194, the limited refundability of financial security is
coupled with a requirement that forfeited amounts be applied to reduce the TSP’s rate base. This
combination produces a materially different outcome. Specifically, the rule:
    1. Permits collection of substantial funds prior to completion of interconnection studies and
       prior to determination of actual system impacts;

    2. Results in retention of those funds even where no corresponding interconnection facilities
       are constructed or stranded costs are incurred; and

    3. Directs that retained amounts be applied in a manner that affects system-wide cost recovery
       through rate base treatment.

        When combined with the requirement that forfeited amounts be applied to reduce
transmission rate base, the financial framework no longer operates solely as an interconnection
cost recovery mechanism. Instead, it introduces a structure that affects system-wide cost recovery
outcomes, which are typically evaluated within the ratemaking framework governed by PURA
Chapter 36.

        It is this interaction—rather than any single provision in isolation—that gives rise to the
principal legal and structural concern. The non-refundable component of intermediate-stage
financial security effectively enables the rule to operate as a mechanism through which funds are
collected from interconnecting customers and subsequently used to offset transmission system
costs, irrespective of cost causation or project-specific impacts.

        Stated differently, the ratemaking effect identified above is not incidental; it is contingent
upon, and driven by, the forfeiture framework embedded in the intermediate agreement
requirements. Absent that forfeiture structure, financial security would remain appropriately



                                                  7
 limited to its role as a risk mitigation and cost recovery tool. With it, the rule extends beyond those
functions and introduces a mechanism with direct implications for transmission cost recovery and
rate base treatment.

        This outcome raises concerns regarding alignment with the statutory framework. PURA §
37.0561 directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. A
structure that imposes substantial non-refundable financial exposure in advance of cost
incurrence—and then applies those funds to system-wide cost recovery—extends beyond those
objectives and is not closely tied to the underlying purposes of cost causation or risk mitigation.

        Therefore, Cholla recommends that the Commission evaluate these provisions collectively
and revise the proposed rule to ensure that:
     1. Financial security remains primarily refundable except to the extent necessary to cover
        identifiable, non-cancellable costs; and

     2. Any treatment of retained funds for ratemaking purposes is not pre-determined within the
        interconnection rule and instead remains subject to appropriate consideration in a future
        ratemaking context.

        Addressing these issues in combination will ensure that the financial framework remains
grounded in cost causation and project-specific risk, while avoiding unintended ratemaking effects
and preserving alignment with the Commission’s statutory mandate under PURA.

                 III.    Practical Effects of the Proposed Financial Structure

A.      System-Level Study Outcomes

        The key problem with the current draft rule is a fatal flaw in its structure: it requires large
load customers to post a substantial per-megawatt financial security deposit at the Intermediate
Agreement stage—currently contemplated at $50,000 per MW—before any interconnection
studies are performed, combined with the risk that most of that deposit will not be returned even
if the study results produce unviable projects. This requirement forces developers to commit
significant capital based on assumptions about system capability that cannot be confirmed until
after the Batch Study process is completed.




                                                  8
     At the beginning of the process, developers are required to make major financial commitments
based on their expectations of what the system can support. However, those expectations are often
incomplete because the developer does not have visibility into:

    ·   other projects in the same area,
    ·   how those projects interact with each other, or
    ·   how system constraints will ultimately be resolved.

    This creates a situation where developers must commit large amounts of money before they
have reliable information.

    A simple example shows how this plays out in practice.

    Assume four different developers each acquire land near a large 345 kV switching station.
Based on experience, each developer reasonably believes that the station can ultimately support
around 1,000 MW of load.

    Three of the developers submit phased load ramps of 250 MW per year from 2028 through
2031. A fourth developer, recognizing that the current rules do not require realistic ramp timing,
submits a request for the full 1,000 MW in 2027.

    None of these developers are aware of each other due to confidentiality rules. They are also
unaware that other developers in the broader area have submitted an additional 10,000 MW of load
requests at nearby facilities.

    Each developer is then required to post $50,000 per MW, resulting in a $50 million deposit for
each project.

    During the Batch Study process, ERCOT evaluates all of the projects together and determines
that, due to transmission constraints, none of the requested load can be served in the originally
proposed timeframes. Instead, the only feasible solution is to delay all of the capacity to a much
later date, such as 2033.

    As a result, each developer receives a revised load ramp showing 1,000 MW of service
beginning in 2033 instead of the original phased schedule.


                                                 9
      From a commercial standpoint, this outcome renders the projects uneconomic. The developers
must either accept a materially worse outcome than they planned for or withdraw from the process.

     If they withdraw, a substantial portion of their deposit is retained. The current rule only allows
for a 20% refund if the load withdraws, so each developer loses $40 million, even though:

     ·   no facilities have been built,
     ·   no stranded costs have been incurred, and
     ·   the change in outcome was driven by system-wide study results that were unknowable at
         the time of the initial request.

         What has happened with the fourth developer illustrates the unintended consequences of
this structure. Because he front-loaded his request, he was able to secure 200 MW in 2027. The
remaining 800 MW was still subject to the same transmission constraints affecting the other
projects, resulting in a revised load ramp of 200 MW in 2027 and 800 MW in 2033.

         This leaves the fourth developer with at least partial economic viability. While 200 MW
alone is not sufficient to support the full project value, it allows the developer to continue moving
forward rather than abandon the project entirely. Critically, instead of losing $40 million like the
other developers, he proceeds with development.

         The outcome sends a clear signal: it does not pay to be responsible and provide a realistic
load ramp. Instead, the only way to preserve a chance at economic viability is to front-load the
request as aggressively as possible.

B.       Upfront Payment Without Feasibility Information

         To illustrate the same issue in a simpler and more relatable way, consider the following
example:

         Imagine Texas changed the rules for buying a truck.

         Every dealership in Texas now requires the same process. Before anyone checks inventory,
you must pay the full purchase price up front — $50,000. You also have to specify exactly what
you want: model, color, trim package, accessories, everything.


                                                  10
          But the dealer cannot tell you at that point whether the truck you need will actually be
available when you need it. Instead, every order in Texas is sent to a central office. That office
waits until all orders are in, looks at statewide inventory and supply constraints, and only then
decides what each customer can get and when.

         A few people may get a truck right away. Most are told they can get their truck in six years.

You need the truck now, not six years from now, so you cancel the order. Texas then sends back
$10,000 of your $50,000 and keeps the other $40,000, even though no truck was delivered and the
reason you canceled was that the system could not provide what you needed on the timeline you
requested.

         Now imagine Oklahoma continues to use a rational process. The dealer first checks whether
it can actually provide the truck you want and when for a small $200 processing fee. Then you
decide whether to move forward. You are not forced to risk $40,000 just to find out the answer is
no.

         Which state do you think people will buy in? If you multiply all of these numbers by 1,000,
you essentially have the structure of the Commission’s proposal.




C.       Resulting Market Behavior and Risk

         A further concern is the mismatch between market expectations and the actual function of
the interconnection study process.

         There appears to be an assumption among some stakeholders that posting financial security
will result in ERCOT delivering the requested load profile. In practice, however, the study process
determines what the system can support—not what any individual developer requests. This
disconnect creates a structural mismatch:
      1. Developers commit capital based on requested load assumptions;

      2. The study process produces system-driven outcomes that may materially differ from those
         assumptions; and



                                                  11
      3. Financial consequences are imposed when those outcomes render projects infeasible.

        Developers with a clear understanding of this dynamic are likely to decline participation
under these conditions, while others may proceed without fully appreciating the associated risk.
This dynamic increases the likelihood of: (i) market confusion; (ii) disputes regarding study
outcomes and financial consequences; and (iii) reduced participation by experienced developers.

D.      Implications for Reliability and Policy Objectives

        While the coordinated study framework represents a meaningful advancement in planning
for large load growth, coupling that framework with substantial, partially non-refundable financial
commitments at the pre-study stage introduces risk that is not necessary to achieve the
Commission’s statutory objectives.

        PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish standards that support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. A
financial structure that imposes significant, non-refundable exposure prior to cost incurrence and
prior to feasibility determination extends beyond those objectives and may discourage efficient
project development.

E.      Recommended Approach

        To better align the rule with statutory objectives and practical realities, Cholla recommends
that the Commission:
     1. Defer material non-refundable financial commitments until after completion of the
        interconnection study and execution of the interconnection agreement;

     2. Limit early-stage financial security to amounts necessary to cover study costs and
        demonstrable pre-construction expenditures; and

     3. Ensure that any forfeiture of financial security is tied to project-specific cost incurrence or
        developer-controlled actions, rather than system-wide study outcomes.

This approach preserves appropriate financial discipline while ensuring that financial exposure
remains proportionate to identifiable risk and consistent with cost-causation principles.

                          IV.     Evaluation of Stated Policy Objectives



                                                  12
         The financial structure reflected in the proposed rule—particularly the limited refundability
of financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage—appears intended to advance
several policy objectives, including: (i) screening out non-viable or speculative (“zombie”)
projects; (ii) protecting existing customers from bearing transmission system costs attributable to
large load interconnections; and (iii) managing the administrative and analytical burden associated
with interconnection studies. Each of these objectives is reasonable and consistent with the
Commission’s statutory mandate under PURA § 37.0561. However, as structured, the proposed
framework does not effectively achieve these objectives and, in certain respects, may undermine
them.

A.      Screening of Non-Viable (“Zombie”) Projects

        The concern regarding speculative or non-viable projects is well-founded. Projects that
lack a realistic path to interconnection or that are not supported by sufficient financial capability
can impose inefficiencies on the study process and complicate system planning.

        However, the proposed rule already incorporates a primary and effective screening
mechanism: the requirement that a large load customer post substantial financial security at the
intermediate agreement stage as a condition to initiating the interconnection study. The magnitude
of this requirement—$50,000 per MW of requested peak demand—serves as a meaningful
indicator of project seriousness and financial capability.

        Where a developer is able to post financial security at this level, the project has, by
definition, demonstrated a degree of financial commitment that distinguishes it from speculative
or non-viable requests. In that context, the incremental introduction of substantial non-refundable
forfeiture does not materially improve screening effectiveness.

        Rather, the appropriate mechanism to ensure that projects reflect genuine commitment is
the transition from refundable financial security to binding, non-refundable obligations after the
interconnection study has been completed and project feasibility has been established. At that
stage, developers have access to the information necessary to make informed investment decisions,
and financial commitments can be appropriately aligned with actual system impacts and cost
exposure.



                                                 13
         By contrast, imposing non-refundable financial exposure prior to completion of the study
process does not enhance screening. It instead introduces financial risk that is not tied to feasibility,
cost incurrence, or developer conduct.

B.      Market Effects and Developer Behavior

        The proposed financial structure also creates incentives that may distort developer behavior
in ways that are inconsistent with efficient system planning.

        Because financial exposure is driven in part by the timing and magnitude of requested load,
and because forfeiture may occur based on study outcomes that differ from initial assumptions,
developers may be incentivized to accelerate or front-load load requests to secure earlier allocation
or submit less conservative load ramp assumptions to preserve optionality.

        Conversely, developers that provide realistic, phased load ramps aligned with actual
development timelines may be disadvantaged if study results delay service or alter project
economics. This creates a structural imbalance in which prudent and accurate project development
assumptions may be penalized relative to more aggressive or speculative approaches.

        In addition, the proposed structure may affect participation decisions. Developers with
experience in ERCOT’s study processes and an understanding of the uncertainty inherent in
system-wide evaluations are likely to decline participation under a framework that imposes
substantial non-refundable financial exposure prior to feasibility determination. At the same time,
participants who are less familiar with these dynamics may proceed, only to encounter materially
different study outcomes and associated financial consequences. This dynamic increases the
likelihood of:
     1. Misaligned expectations regarding study outcomes;

     2. Disputes arising from differences between requested and deliverable service; and

     3. Volatility in project participation and development pipelines.

Such outcomes are not necessary to achieve the Commission’s objectives and may, in practice,
introduce inefficiencies into both the market and the planning process.

C.      Planning and Study Process Considerations


                                                   14
         The proposed structure also appears intended, in part, to manage the burden associated with
interconnection studies. However, the rule already includes mechanisms that directly address
study-related costs and administrative effort.

        Specifically, the proposed rule requires large load customers to pay study fees to cover the
costs of conducting interconnection studies, with provisions for true-up to actual costs where
necessary. These fees are appropriately designed to ensure that the costs of the study process are
borne by the requesting customer, consistent with cost-causation principles.

        Moreover, the transition toward a coordinated or batch study framework is intended to
improve efficiency by reducing the need for repeated, project-specific studies, and enabling
system-level evaluation of multiple requests in a single process.

        To the extent that planning complexity remains, it is driven primarily by modeling
assumptions, including the interaction of load growth with generation development and
transmission expansion, rather than by the volume of individual requests alone.

        In this context, the introduction of substantial non-refundable financial exposure at the
intermediate stage does not directly address the underlying drivers of planning complexity or study
burden. Instead, it reallocates financial risk to developers without materially reducing the
analytical requirements of the study process. The rule therefore moves beyond interconnection
cost recovery and into system cost recovery, which is governed by PURA Chapter 36.

D.      Summary

        In summary, while the objectives underlying the proposed financial structure are
appropriate, the current design does not effectively advance those objectives. The combination of
substantial upfront financial security and limited refundability:

     1. Does not materially improve screening of non-viable projects beyond what is already
        achieved through existing financial requirements;

     2. Creates incentives that may distort developer behavior and reduce the accuracy of
        information provided in interconnection requests; and

     3. Does not directly address the core drivers of planning complexity or study burden.



                                                 15
        Accordingly, Cholla recommends that the Commission refine the proposed framework to
ensure that financial requirements are calibrated to actual system risk, tied to project-specific cost
incurrence, and implemented at stages of the process where developers have sufficient information
to make informed decisions. Such refinements would better align the rule with the Commission’s
statutory objectives under PURA § 37.0561 while preserving efficient and reliable system
planning.

       For these reasons, the current structure does not align with the statutory framework
governing interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561 and raises additional considerations
regarding the appropriate separation between interconnection requirements and transmission cost
recovery mechanisms.

                       VI.    Proposed Refinement to Financial Structure

       A targeted refinement to the proposed rule would address the principal concerns identified
above while preserving the Commission’s core objectives. Specifically, following completion of
the interconnection study (including any applicable batch study process), financial security posted
at the intermediate agreement stage should be:
   1. Fully refundable in the event the large load customer elects not to proceed based on study
      results; or

   2. Credited toward actual interconnection costs, including CIAC and other project-specific
      expenditures, where the large load customer elects to proceed.

       This approach restores alignment with fundamental cost-causation principles by ensuring
that financial obligations correspond to identifiable system impacts and incurred costs. It also
eliminates the economic distortions inherent in imposing substantial non-refundable financial
exposure prior to feasibility determination.

       Importantly, this refinement does not diminish the role of financial security as a mechanism
to demonstrate commitment. Large load customers would remain required to post meaningful
financial security at the outset, thereby ensuring that only projects with credible financial backing
advance into the study process. However, developers would not be subject to substantial financial
loss based on system-wide study outcomes that cannot be known in advance and are not within the
developer’s control.


                                                 16
        This revised structure preserves discipline within the interconnection process while
ensuring that financial exposure remains proportionate to actual costs and risks, rather than to
uncertainty inherent in the study process itself.

                                        VII.    Conclusion

       The Commission has made meaningful progress in developing a framework capable of
managing the scale and complexity of large load interconnection in ERCOT. The transition to a
coordinated batch study process represents a necessary and constructive step toward improving
planning efficiency and maintaining system reliability. Cholla supports the direction of this effort.
However, as currently structured, the proposed rule introduces two interdependent elements that,
when combined, produce a central structural concern and warrant targeted refinement.

       First, the rule incorporates provisions with direct ratemaking implications by requiring that
certain retained financial amounts be applied as an offset to transmission rate base, thereby
affecting system-wide cost recovery outside the context of a Chapter 36 ratemaking proceeding.

       Second, the rule imposes substantial non-refundable financial commitments at the
intermediate agreement stage—prior to completion of interconnection studies and without a clear
connection to incurred costs or identifiable stranded infrastructure risk.

       Together, these elements create a misalignment between financial exposure and available
information—including the fact that financial outcomes are driven by system-wide study results
rather than project-specific conduct or cost incurrence—and introduce unnecessary risk and
distortion into project development and participation. In combination, they transform financial
security from a mechanism intended to ensure cost recovery and mitigate stranded cost risk into
one that can impose material financial consequences unrelated to those statutory objectives.

       These concerns reflect a broader misalignment with the statutory framework in PURA §
37.0561, which is focused on project-specific cost recovery, protection against stranded
infrastructure, and support for business development while maintaining system reliability. The
outcomes described above are not required to achieve those objectives. The rule already includes
effective mechanisms—financial security, CIAC, and recovery of actual costs—to ensure project
viability, protect existing customers, and support efficient system planning.


                                                    17
         A targeted refinement addresses these concerns. Following completion of the
interconnection study, financial security should be:
    1. Fully refundable if the project does not proceed; or

    2. Applied to actual interconnection costs if the project advances.

        This approach preserves appropriate financial discipline, aligns with cost-causation
principles, eliminates unnecessary non-refundable exposure tied to system-wide uncertainty, and
maintains consistency with the statutory framework governing interconnection standards.

        With this adjustment, the Commission can finalize a framework that is operationally
effective, legally sound, and capable of supporting continued large-scale investment while
maintaining reliability and protecting existing customers.

        Cholla believes that creating good policy is like choosing what to do on Date Night. It’s
always good to start with a list of things that are legal.

                                       I.     Introduction


       Cholla, Inc. ("Cholla") appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on proposed 16
Tex. Admin. Code ("TAC") § 25.194 implementing Public Utility Regulatory Act ("PURA") §
37.0561 regarding interconnection standards for large load customers in the ERCOT region. As a
developer of large-scale load infrastructure in Texas, Cholla is committed to supporting a reliable,
efficient, and transparent interconnection framework that enables continued economic growth
while maintaining system integrity.

       Cholla supports the Commission's objective of ensuring that large load interconnection
requests are grounded in demonstrably viable and committed projects. The scale and pace of large
load development in ERCOT necessitate a structured framework that appropriately balances
business development, system reliability, and protection of existing customers. In particular, the
transition toward a coordinated or batch study process represents a meaningful and necessary
evolution in transmission planning.

       At the same time, targeted refinements to the proposed rule are necessary to ensure that
financial requirements remain appropriately calibrated, non-duplicative, and closely aligned with
actual system risk and cost incurrence. As currently structured, certain provisions-particularly
those governing financial security at the intermediate agreement stage and the treatment of retained
funds-introduce outcomes that are not closely tied to cost causation or stranded infrastructure
risk and that may have broader implications for transmission cost recovery.

       These comments focus on two interdependent aspects of the proposed framework: (i) the
non-refundable structure of financial security prior to completion of interconnection studies, and
(ii) the required treatment of retained funds in a manner that affects transmission rate base. As

 discussed below, the interaction of these elements results in a financial structure that extends
beyond proj ect-specific interconnection cost recovery and introduces unintended economic and
structural effects.

         Cholla respectfully submits that these issues can be addressed through targeted
refinement-without altering the overall structure or objectives ofthe rule-to ensure that the final
framework remains consistent with PURA § 37.0561, grounded in cost-causation principles, and
capable of supporting continued investment in large load infrastructure while maintaining system

               II.     Structural Concerns with Proposed Financial Framework

A.       Ratemaking Implications of Proposed Financial Treatment

         As proposed in Staff's Proposal for Publication ("PFP"), § 25.194 includes provisions that
extend beyond the establishment of interconnection standards and, as structured, introduce
elements that constitute ratemaking in substance by determining how funds are applied to rate base
outside of a PURA Chapter 36 proceeding.

         In particular, the rule requires that certain payments collected from large load customers-
including amounts derived from financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage-be
transferred to the interconnecting Transmission Service Provider ("TSP") and applied as an offset
to the TSP's rate base in a future rate proceeding. As a result, those amounts no longer function
solely as mechanisms to ensure recovery of proj ect-specific interconnection costs or to protect
against stranded infrastructure risk. Instead, they directly affect the level of transmission system
costs ultimately recovered from ratepayers. In practice, many large load interconnection requests
are initiated by developers or proj ect sponsors that are not themselves the ultimate end-use
customer and may never take service on the ERCOT system. The rule therefore requires entities
that are not customers of the ERCOT system-and may never become customers-to fund
transmission system costs through forfeited financial security.

         Under PURA Chapter 36, ratemaking is governed by a structured framework. The
Commission is authorized to establish and regulate rates and to determine customer classifications




                                                  2
 and applicability of rates.1 Rates must be just and reasonable and may not be unreasonably
preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. 2 In setting rates, the Commission must establish the
utility's overall revenue requirement at a level that provides a reasonable opportunity to earn a
return on invested capital used and useful in providing service. 3 This process necessarily includes
determination of revenues and expenses and the allocation of costs in accordance with established
ratemaking principles.4

       Although the Commission retains authority to adopt rules that may influence ratemaking
outcomes, as proposed, 16 TAC § 25.194 effectively prescribes the treatment of specific funds
within future rate base calculations without the benefit of those procedural and evidentiary
safeguards. In a ratemaking context, the utility bears the burden of demonstrating that proposed
rates are just and reasonable.5 By contrast, the proposed rule would predetermine that certain
payments are applied to reduce rate base outside ofthat framework.

       This concern is further underscored by the statutory requirement that rate base be grounded
in property that is used and useful in providing service.6 To the extent payments collected from
large load customers are retained and applied to reduce transmission rate base irrespective of
whether they correspond to used and useful utility investment, they function as a system-wide cost
recovery mechanism rather than a project-specific interconnection safeguard. This disconnect
further demonstrates that the retained funds are not tied to specific utility investment used and
useful in providing service, but instead operate as a generalized funding mechanism.

       These ratemaking implications should be considered in light of the statutory framework
under which this rule is adopted. PURA § 35.004 requires that large load customers contribute to
the recovery of the utility's costs to interconnect that customer, and PURA § 37.0561 directs the
Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business development, minimize
stranded infrastructure costs, and maintain system reliability. These provisions are focused on

        Cholla does not dispute the Commission's authority to determine rate base treatment under

of transmission system costs.

B.      Non-Refundable Financial Commitments at the Intermediate Stage

        Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 requires large load customers to post substantial financial
security at the intermediate agreement stage--prior to initiation of the interconnection study-in
the amount of $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand. This requirement, in combination with
the rule's withdrawal and forfeiture provisions, introduces a structure that imposes material non-
refundable financial exposure before a project's technical feasibility, cost profile, or deliverability
has been established.

        Consistent with PURA §§ 35.004 and 37.0561, financial security should be calibrated to
ensure recovery of incurred interconnection costs and protection against identifiable stranded
infrastructure risk, rather than to create independent financial exposure unrelated to those statutory


                                                  4
 objectives.

        Specifically, under § 25.194(d)(10), a large load customer must post financial security as a
condition to initiating the interconnection study. Ifthe customer subsequently withdraws its request
or is unable to proceed-whether due to study results, system constraints, or other external
factors-the rule requires that the interconnecting utility first apply the financial security to any
outstanding costs and then refund only 20% of any remaining balance, with the remaining 80%
transferred to the TSP and applied as an offset to rate base.

       As structured, this framework results in substantial non-refundable forfeiture even in
circumstances where:
    1. No interconnection facilities have been constructed;

   2. No stranded infrastructure costs have been incurred; and

    3. The outcome of the interconnection study or broader system conditions renders the project
       infeasible or materially altered from its original assumptions.

       This allocation of risk is not aligned with the statutory objectives underlying PURA §
37.0561. That provision directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that
minimize the potential for stranded infrastructure costs while maintaining system reliability. The
financial security requirement, however, extends beyond protection against identifiable cost
exposure and instead places significant financial risk on the developer prior to the point at which
such risk can be reasonably evaluated.

       In effect, the rule requires large load customers to commit substantial capital before they
have access to the very information-study results, upgrade requirements, cost estimates, and
deliverability constraints-necessary to assess project viability. The resulting forfeiture risk is
therefore driven not by developer conduct, failure to perform, or incurred system costs, but by the
outcome of system-wide study processes and planning determinations that are outside the control
of the large load customer.

       This structure transforms financial security from a tool intended to (i) ensure cost recovery
for interconnection-related expenditures, and (ii) protect utilities and ratepayers from stranded
infrastructure risk, into a mechanism that imposes material, non-refundable financial exposure in



                                                  5
 advance of those risks being realized or even quantified.

        Moreover, because the majority of forfeited amounts are ultimately transferred to the TSP
and applied as an offset to rate base, the forfeiture is not limited to recovery of project-specific
costs, but instead operates as a broader funding mechanism affecting transmission system cost
recovery. This further underscores that the current structure is not narrowly tailored to the statutory
purposes of cost causation and stranded cost protection.

        Accordingly, Cholla recommends that the Commission revise the intermediate-stage
financial security framework to better align with PURA § 37.0561 by:
     1. Limiting non-refundable exposure at the intermediate stage to amounts directly tied to
        incurred or non-cancellable costs;

     2. Preserving a higher degree of refundability until completion of the interconnection study
        and execution of the interconnection agreement; and

     3. Ensuring that forfeiture is triggered by demonstrable cost incurrence or developer-driven
        actions, rather than by system-wide study outcomes or feasibility determinations.

        A revised structure that ties financial exposure to actual cost incurrence and proj ect-specific
risk would maintain appropriate discipline and commitment from interconnecting customers while
avoiding unnecessary barriers to development and preserving alignment with the statutory
obj ectives of reliability, cost causation, and support for business development in Texas.


C.      Interaction of Financial Structure and Ratemaking Treatment

        The concerns identified above regarding (1) the ratemaking implications of the proposed
financial treatment, and (2) the non-refundable structure of financial security at the intermediate
agreement stage are not independent. Rather, they operate together as an integrated mechanism
that produces outcomes extending beyond the scope of interconnection standards contemplated
under PURA §§ 35.004 and 37.0561.

        As proposed, the rule requires large load customers to post substantial financial security
prior to the initiation of interconnection studies and, in the event of withdrawal or non-utilization,
directs that only a limited portion of the remaining balance be refunded, with the majority
transferred to the TSP and applied as an offset to rate base. This interaction between early-stage
financial commitments and downstream ratemaking treatment is central to the structure and effect


                                                   6
 of the rule.

        If financial security at the intermediate stage were structured to remain largely
refundable-subject to deduction only for demonstrable, proj ect-specific costs incurred by the
interconnecting utility-the financial framework would function in a manner consistent with
traditional interconnection principles. In that case, financial security would serve its intended
purposes of ensuring cost recovery for interconnection-related expenditures and protecting against
stranded infrastructure risk, consistent with PURA.

        However, under proposed § 25.194, the limited refundability of financial security is
coupled with a requirement that forfeited amounts be applied to reduce the TSP's rate base. This
combination produces a materially different outcome. Specifically, the rule:
    1. Permits collection of substantial funds prior to completion of interconnection studies and
        prior to determination of actual system impacts;

    2. Results in retention of those funds even where no corresponding interconnection facilities
        are constructed or stranded costs are incurred; and

    3. Directs that retained amounts be applied in a manner that affects system-wide cost recovery
        through rate base treatment.

        When combined with the requirement that forfeited amounts be applied to reduce
transmission rate base, the financial framework no longer operates solely as an interconnection
cost recovery mechanism. Instead, it introduces a structure that affects system-wide cost recovery
outcomes, which are typically evaluated within the ratemaking framework governed by PURA
Chapter 36.

        It is this interaction-rather than any single provision in isolation-that gives rise to the
principal legal and structural concern. The non-refundable component of intermediate-stage
financial security effectively enables the rule to operate as a mechanism through which funds are
collected from interconnecting customers and subsequently used to offset transmission system
costs, irrespective of cost causation or proj ect-specific impacts.

        Stated differently, the ratemaking effect identified above is not incidental; it is contingent
upon, and driven by, the forfeiture framework embedded in the intermediate agreement
requirements. Absent that forfeiture structure, financial security would remain appropriately



                                                   7
 limited to its role as a risk mitigation and cost recovery tool. With it, the rule extends beyond those
functions and introduces a mechanism with direct implications for transmission cost recovery and
rate base treatment.

        This outcome raises concerns regarding alignment with the statutory framework. PURA §
37.0561 directs the Commission to establish interconnection standards that support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. A
structure that imposes substantial non-refundable financial exposure in advance of cost
incurrence-and then applies those funds to system-wide cost recovery-extends beyond those
objectives and is not closely tied to the underlying purposes of cost causation or risk mitigation.

        Therefore, Cholla recommends that the Commission evaluate these provisions collectively
and revise the proposed rule to ensure that:
     1. Financial security remains primarily refundable except to the extent necessary to cover
        identifiable, non-cancellable costs; and

     2. Any treatment of retained funds for ratemaking purposes is not pre-determined within the
        interconnection rule and instead remains subj ect to appropriate consideration in a future
        ratemaking context.

        Addressing these issues in combination will ensure that the financial framework remains
grounded in cost causation and project-specific risk, while avoiding unintended ratemaking effects
and preserving alignment with the Commission's statutory mandate under PURA.

                  III.   Practical Effects of the Proposed Financial Structure

A.      System-Level Study Outcomes

        The key problem with the current draft rule is a fatal flaw in its structure: it requires large
load customers to post a substantial per-megawatt financial security deposit at the Intermediate
Agreement stage-currently contemplated at $50,000 per MW-before any interconnection
studies are performed, combined with the risk that most of that deposit will not be returned even
if the study results produce unviable projects. This requirement forces developers to commit
significant capital based on assumptions about system capability that cannot be confirmed until
after the Batch Study process is completed.




                                                   8
     At the beginning ofthe process, developers are required to make major financial commitments
based on their expectations ofwhat the system can support. However, those expectations are often
incomplete because the developer does not have visibility into:

        other proj ects in the same area,
        how those proj ects interact with each other, or
        how system constraints will ultimately be resolved.

    This creates a situation where developers must commit large amounts of money before they
have reliable information.

    A simple example shows how this plays out in practice.

    Assume four different developers each acquire land near a large 345 kV switching station.
Based on experience, each developer reasonably believes that the station can ultimately support
around 1,000 MW of load.

    Three of the developers submit phased load ramps of 250 MW per year from 2028 through
2031. A fourth developer, recognizing that the current rules do not require realistic ramp timing,
submits a request for the full 1,000 MW in 2027.

    None of these developers are aware of each other due to confidentiality rules. They are also
unaware that other developers in the broader area have submitted an additional 10,000 MW of load
requests at nearby facilities.

    Each developer is then required to post $50,000 per MW, resulting in a $50 million deposit for
each proj ect.

    During the Batch Study process, ERCOT evaluates all of the projects together and determines
that, due to transmission constraints, none of the requested load can be served in the originally
proposed timeframes. Instead, the only feasible solution is to delay all of the capacity to a much
later date, such as 2033.

    As a result, each developer receives a revised load ramp showing 1,000 MW of service
beginning in 2033 instead ofthe original phased schedule.


                                                  9
      From a commercial standpoint, this outcome renders the projects uneconomic. The developers
must either accept a materially worse outcome than they planned for or withdraw from the process.

     If they withdraw, a substantial portion oftheir deposit is retained. The current rule only allows
for a 20% refund if the load withdraws, so each developer loses $40 million, even though:

        no facilities have been built,
        no stranded costs have been incurred, and
        the change in outcome was driven by system-wide study results that were unknowable at
        the time of the initial request.

        What has happened with the fourth developer illustrates the unintended consequences of
this structure. Because he front-loaded his request, he was able to secure 200 MW in 2027. The
remaining 800 MW was still subject to the same transmission constraints affecting the other
projects, resulting in a revised load ramp of 200 MW in 2027 and 800 MW in 2033.

        This leaves the fourth developer with at least partial economic viability. While 200 MW
alone is not sufficient to support the full project value, it allows the developer to continue moving
forward rather than abandon the proj ect entirely. Critically, instead of losing $40 million like the
other developers, he proceeds with development.

        The outcome sends a clear signal: it does not pay to be responsible and provide a realistic
load ramp. Instead, the only way to preserve a chance at economic viability is to front-load the
request as aggressively as possible.

B.      Upfront Payment Without Feasibility Information

        To illustrate the same issue in a simpler and more relatable way, consider the following
example:

        Imagine Texas changed the rules for buying a truck.


        Every dealership in Texas now requires the same process. Before anyone checks inventory,
you must pay the full purchase price up front - $50,000. You also have to specify exactly what
you want: model, color, trim package, accessories, everything.


                                                  10
          But the dealer cannot tell you at that point whether the truck you need will actually be
available when you need it. Instead, every order in Texas is sent to a central office. That office
waits until all orders are in, looks at statewide inventory and supply constraints, and only then
decides what each customer can get and when.

         A few people may get a truck right away. Most are told they can get their truck in six years.

You need the truck now, not six years from now, so you cancel the order. Texas then sends back
$10,000 of your $50,000 and keeps the other $40,000, even though no truck was delivered and the
reason you canceled was that the system could not provide what you needed on the timeline you
requested.

         Now imagine Oklahoma continues to use a rational process. The dealer first checks whether
it can actually provide the truck you want and when for a small $200 processing fee. Then you
decide whether to move forward. You are not forced to risk $40,000 just to find out the answer is
no.



         Which state do you think people will buy in? Ifyou multiply all ofthese numbers by 1,000,
you essentially have the structure ofthe Commission's proposal.




C.       Resulting Market Behavior and Risk

         A further concern is the mismatch between market expectations and the actual function of
the interconnection study process.

         There appears to be an assumption among some stakeholders that posting financial security
will result in ERCOT delivering the requested load profile. In practice, however, the study process
determines what the system can support-not what any individual developer requests. This
disconnect creates a structural mismatch:
      1. Developers commit capital based on requested load assumptions;

      2. The study process produces system-driven outcomes that may materially differ from those
         assumptions; and



                                                  11
      3. Financial consequences are imposed when those outcomes render proj ects infeasible.


        Developers with a clear understanding of this dynamic are likely to decline participation
under these conditions, while others may proceed without fully appreciating the associated risk.
This dynamic increases the likelihood of: (i) market confusion; (ii) disputes regarding study
outcomes and financial consequences; and (iii) reduced participation by experienced developers.

D.      Implications for Reliability and Policy Objectives

        While the coordinated study framework represents a meaningful advancement in planning
for large load growth, coupling that framework with substantial, partially non-refundable financial
commitments at the pre-study stage introduces risk that is not necessary to achieve the
Commission's statutory objectives.

        PURA § 37.0561 directs the Commission to establish standards that support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability. A
financial structure that imposes significant, non-refundable exposure prior to cost incurrence and
prior to feasibility determination extends beyond those objectives and may discourage efficient
proj ect development.

E.      Recommended Approach

        To better align the rule with statutory obj ectives and practical realities, Cholla recommends
that the Commission:
     1. Defer material non-refundable financial commitments until after completion of the
        interconnection study and execution of the interconnection agreement;

     2. Limit early-stage financial security to amounts necessary to cover study costs and
        demonstrable pre-construction expenditures; and

     3. Ensure that any forfeiture of financial security is tied to project-specific cost incurrence or
        developer-controlled actions, rather than system-wide study outcomes.

This approach preserves appropriate financial discipline while ensuring that financial exposure
remains proportionate to identifiable risk and consistent with cost-causation principles.

                          IV.     Evaluation of Stated Policy Objectives



                                                  12
         The financial structure reflected in the proposed rule--particularly the limited refundability
of financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage-appears intended to advance
several policy objectives, including: (i) screening out non-viable or speculative ("zombie")
projects; (ii) protecting existing customers from bearing transmission system costs attributable to
large load interconnections; and (iii) managing the administrative and analytical burden associated
with interconnection studies. Each of these objectives is reasonable and consistent with the
Commission's statutory mandate under PURA § 37.0561. However, as structured, the proposed
framework does not effectively achieve these obj ectives and, in certain respects, may undermine
them.

A.      Screening of Non-Viable ("Zombie") Projects

        The concern regarding speculative or non-viable projects is well-founded. Projects that
lack a realistic path to interconnection or that are not supported by sufficient financial capability
can impose inefficiencies on the study process and complicate system planning.

        However, the proposed rule already incorporates a primary and effective screening
mechanism: the requirement that a large load customer post substantial financial security at the
intermediate agreement stage as a condition to initiating the interconnection study. The magnitude
of this requirement-$50,000 per MW of requested peak demand-serves as a meaningful
indicator of proj ect seriousness and financial capability.

        Where a developer is able to post financial security at this level, the project has, by
definition, demonstrated a degree of financial commitment that distinguishes it from speculative
or non-viable requests. In that context, the incremental introduction of substantial non-refundable
forfeiture does not materially improve screening effectiveness.

        Rather, the appropriate mechanism to ensure that proj ects reflect genuine commitment is
the transition from refundable financial security to binding, non-refundable obligations after the
interconnection study has been completed and project feasibility has been established. At that
stage, developers have access to the information necessary to make informed investment decisions,
and financial commitments can be appropriately aligned with actual system impacts and cost
exposure.


                                                  13
         By contrast, imposing non-refundable financial exposure prior to completion of the study
process does not enhance screening. It instead introduces financial risk that is not tied to feasibility,
cost incurrence, or developer conduct.

B.      Market Effects and Developer Behavior


        The proposed financial structure also creates incentives that may distort developerbehavior
in ways that are inconsistent with efficient system planning.

        Because financial exposure is driven in part by the timing and magnitude of requested load,
and because forfeiture may occur based on study outcomes that differ from initial assumptions,
developers may be incentivized to accelerate or front-load load requests to secure earlier allocation
or submit less conservative load ramp assumptions to preserve optionality.

        Conversely, developers that provide realistic, phased load ramps aligned with actual
development timelines may be disadvantaged if study results delay service or alter proj ect
economics. This creates a structural imbalance in which prudent and accurate project development
assumptions may be penalized relative to more aggressive or speculative approaches.

        In addition, the proposed structure may affect participation decisions. Developers with
experience in ERCOT's study processes and an understanding of the uncertainty inherent in
system-wide evaluations are likely to decline participation under a framework that imposes
substantial non-refundable financial exposure prior to feasibility determination. At the same time,
participants who are less familiar with these dynamics may proceed, only to encounter materially
different study outcomes and associated financial consequences. This dynamic increases the
likelihood of:
     1. Misaligned expectations regarding study outcomes;

     2. Disputes arising from differences between requested and deliverable service; and

     3. Volatility in project participation and development pipelines.

Such outcomes are not necessary to achieve the Commission's objectives and may, in practice,
introduce inefficiencies into both the market and the planning process.

C.      Planning and Study Process Considerations


                                                   14
         The proposed structure also appears intended, in part, to manage the burden associated with
interconnection studies. However, the rule already includes mechanisms that directly address
study-related costs and administrative effort.

        Specifically, the proposed rule requires large load customers to pay study fees to cover the
costs of conducting interconnection studies, with provisions for true-up to actual costs where
necessary. These fees are appropriately designed to ensure that the costs of the study process are
borne by the requesting customer, consistent with cost-causation principles.

        Moreover, the transition toward a coordinated or batch study framework is intended to
improve efficiency by reducing the need for repeated, project-specific studies, and enabling
system-level evaluation of multiple requests in a single process.

        To the extent that planning complexity remains, it is driven primarily by modeling
assumptions, including the interaction of load growth with generation development and
transmission expansion, rather than by the volume of individual requests alone.

        In this context, the introduction of substantial non-refundable financial exposure at the
intermediate stage does not directly address the underlying drivers ofplanning complexity or study
burden. Instead, it reallocates financial risk to developers without materially reducing the
analytical requirements of the study process. The rule therefore moves beyond interconnection
cost recovery and into system cost recovery, which is governed by PURA Chapter 36.

D.      Summary

        In summary, while the obj ectives underlying the proposed financial structure are
appropriate, the current design does not effectively advance those obj ectives. The combination of
substantial upfront financial security and limited refundability:

     1. Does not materially improve screening of non-viable projects beyond what is already
        achieved through existing financial requirements;

     2. Creates incentives that may distort developer behavior and reduce the accuracy of
        information provided in interconnection requests; and

     3. Does not directly address the core drivers of planning complexity or study burden.



                                                 15
        Accordingly, Cholla recommends that the Commission refine the proposed framework to
ensure that financial requirements are calibrated to actual system risk, tied to proj ect-specific cost
incurrence, and implemented at stages ofthe process where developers have sufficient information
to make informed decisions. Such refinements would better align the rule with the Commission's
statutory objectives under PURA § 37.0561 while preserving efficient and reliable system
planning.

       For these reasons, the current structure does not align with the statutory framework
governing interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561 and raises additional considerations
regarding the appropriate separation between interconnection requirements and transmission cost
recovery mechani sms.

                       VI.    Proposed Refinement to Financial Structure

       A targeted refinement to the proposed rule would address the principal concerns identified
above while preserving the Commission's core objectives. Specifically, following completion of
the interconnection study (including any applicable batch study process), financial security posted
at the intermediate agreement stage should be:
    1. Fully refundable in the event the large load customer elects not to proceed based on study
       results; or

   2. Credited toward actual interconnection costs, including CIAC and other project-specific
      expenditures, where the large load customer elects to proceed.

       This approach restores alignment with fundamental cost-causation principles by ensuring
that financial obligations correspond to identifiable system impacts and incurred costs. It also
eliminates the economic distortions inherent in imposing substantial non-refundable financial
exposure prior to feasibility determination.

       Importantly, this refinement does not diminish the role offinancial security as a mechanism
to demonstrate commitment. Large load customers would remain required to post meaningful
financial security at the outset, thereby ensuring that only proj ects with credible financial backing
advance into the study process. However, developers would not be subject to substantial financial
loss based on system-wide study outcomes that cannot be known in advance and are not within the
developer's control.


                                                  16
         This revised structure preserves discipline within the interconnection process while
ensuring that financial exposure remains proportionate to actual costs and risks, rather than to
uncertainty inherent in the study process itself.

                                         VII.       Conclusion

        The Commission has made meaningful progress in developing a framework capable of
managing the scale and complexity of large load interconnection in ERCOT. The transition to a
coordinated batch study process represents a necessary and constructive step toward improving
planning efficiency and maintaining system reliability. Cholla supports the direction ofthis effort.
However, as currently structured, the proposed rule introduces two interdependent elements that,
when combined, produce a central structural concern and warrant targeted refinement.

       First, the rule incorporates provisions with direct ratemaking implications by requiring that
certain retained financial amounts be applied as an offset to transmission rate base, thereby
affecting system-wide cost recovery outside the context of a Chapter 36 ratemaking proceeding.

        Second, the rule imposes substantial non-refundable financial commitments at the
intermediate agreement stage--prior to completion of interconnection studies and without a clear
connection to incurred costs or identifiable stranded infrastructure risk.

        Together, these elements create a misalignment between financial exposure and available
information-including the fact that financial outcomes are driven by system-wide study results
rather than project-specific conduct or cost incurrence-and introduce unnecessary risk and
distortion into project development and participation. In combination, they transform financial
security from a mechanism intended to ensure cost recovery and mitigate stranded cost risk into
one that can impose material financial consequences unrelated to those statutory obj ectives.

        These concerns reflect a broader misalignment with the statutory framework in PURA §
37.0561, which is focused on project-specific cost recovery, protection against stranded
infrastructure, and support for business development while maintaining system reliability. The
outcomes described above are not required to achieve those objectives. The rule already includes
effective mechanisms-financial security, CIAC, and recovery of actual costs-to ensure project
viability, protect existing customers, and support efficient system planning.


                                                     17
         A targeted refinement addresses these concerns.           Following completion of the
interconnection study, financial security should be:
    1. Fully refundable if the project does not proceed; or

   2. Applied to actual interconnection costs if the proj ect advances.

        This approach preserves appropriate financial discipline, aligns with cost-causation
principles, eliminates unnecessary non-refundable exposure tied to system-wide uncertainty, and
maintains consistency with the statutory framework governing interconnection standards.

       With this adjustment, the Commission can finalize a framework that is operationally
effective, legally sound, and capable of supporting continued large-scale investment while
maintaining reliability and protecting existing customers.
